scope: All 48 manuscript writing moves, original-example passages/tables, candidate purposes and player bindings reviewed. Entire article files were structurally checked. This is not a full audio audition, a bar-by-bar analysis of all 144 candidates, or a fresh validation of all external source URLs.

findings.finding: The broader listening selection is not integrated: 44 articles still have no named external listening study in their body; only three have a player.
The three pilot players are prepended before the article. Article prose now explains each, but section-level player placement remains to be implemented.
The five pilot passage windows are broad comparison windows, not verified phrase/section boundaries or completed interval/harmonic transcriptions.
The pilot player bindings had no matching discussion in the three article bodies.
findings.status: fixed with context, source links, original transfer and limits

findings.finding: A repeated Radiohead texture example in article 43 did not implement the planned same-song sonic-setting comparison.
findings.status: replaced by the Joni Mitchell 1969/2000 comparison with primary album identities

findings.finding: The listening guide still includes seven older studies in addition to the three pilots; five of the ten focus on Beatles/Radiohead. It does not yet represent the full approved stylistic breadth.
findings.status: remaining; retain the approved limited placements when replacing the old mix

findings.finding: Applied dominants, borrowed chords, actual voice leading and bridge labels need checked, recording-specific passages before detailed diagrams. Transposition needs editions/recordings that actually preserve interval relationships.
Source-register attribution and chapter metadata had drifted from the manuscript.
findings.status: updated five changed chapter entries, new sources, and stale Radiohead/Beatles used_by bindings

articles.title: Protect the Song's Identity
articles.original_example_review: Seed rhythm and pitch are separated from the instrument carrying them. Platform Three gives identity a second, groove-based context.
articles.fit_reason: Track the opening idea through changed surroundings; identity is broader than choosing one hook.
articles.remaining_checks: Choose a named performance; do not present work notes as a recording.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Begin with What You Have
articles.original_example_review: Word-, melody-, rhythm-, harmony- and sound-led entrances leave the later workflow open.
articles.fit_reason: The band interview can distinguish documented process from an imagined starting route.
articles.remaining_checks: Listen to and cite the relevant interview passage; do not infer chronology from the finished track.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Repeat with a Reason
articles.original_example_review: The seed alternatives preserve four beats while changing pitch or timing; Platform Three uses omission rather than constant novelty.
articles.named_listening_study_in_body: Four Tet — Two Thousand and Seventeen
articles.recommended_anchor: Four Tet — “Two Thousand and Seventeen,” on _New Energy_.
articles.fit_reason: Keep a recognizable figure available while its surrounding texture changes.
articles.remaining_checks: Pilot prose added. Refine the broad opening/later windows and put the player beside this explanation.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Listen Like a Songwriter
articles.original_example_review: Observation, interpretation and a new original test are distinguished.
articles.recommended_anchor: Radiohead — “Everything in Its Right Place,” on _Kid A_.
articles.fit_reason: Separate keyboard, lead voice and processed vocal texture into distinct listening passes.
articles.remaining_checks: Use this reference here rather than repeating the same Radiohead study in the sound-setting article.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Capture Musical Seeds
articles.original_example_review: The capture notes retain durations, tempo context, uncertainty and a next question.
articles.recommended_anchor: Billie Eilish — “everything i wanted,” with FINNEAS.
articles.fit_reason: Original voice memos give direct evidence of what a rough capture preserves.
articles.remaining_checks: The creator interview is a process source; the released song alone cannot establish the workflow.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Finish a Tiny Song
articles.original_example_review: The sixteen-bar miniature has a clear arc, explicit split harmony in its last passage, and is distinguished from the complete lyric.
articles.fit_reason: A short vocal work can communicate a complete idea without a mandatory bridge or large arrangement.
articles.remaining_checks: Map the exact recording; short duration alone does not prove that its form matches the course miniature.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Set the Pace for the Phrase
articles.original_example_review: Beat rate, note density, vocal space and calculated durations are kept separate.
articles.fit_reason: Compare spacious singing with the activity in a repeating backing.
articles.remaining_checks: Count a passage before attaching BPM; do not confuse subdivisions with the shared beat.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Group the Beat Around the Phrase
articles.original_example_review: The rewritten three-beat seed is distinguished from relabeling unchanged events; compound and simple grouping are separate.
articles.fit_reason: Follow a recurring grouping against the vocal rather than treating meter as note counting alone.
articles.remaining_checks: Check the actual grouping and passage in the selected recording before adding a meter diagram.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Make Space Part of the Rhythm
articles.original_example_review: Both rest variants total four beats; silence is counted instead of deleting time.
articles.fit_reason: Compare gaps in a vocal or bass part against what continues elsewhere.
articles.remaining_checks: Specify which part is resting; a gap in one layer is not necessarily complete silence.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Pull an Entrance Across the Beat
articles.original_example_review: The chorus pickup isolates vocal placement before anticipating the harmony as a separate alternative.
articles.fit_reason: A checked ragtime passage can expose offbeat attacks against a clear accompaniment.
articles.remaining_checks: Distinguish syncopation from an anticipatory section entrance; not every offbeat is a pickup.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Give the Groove a Consistent Feel
articles.original_example_review: Uneven pairs, a whole-part delay and cumulative drift are correctly distinguished.
articles.recommended_anchor: Duke Ellington and His Orchestra, featuring Ivie Anderson — “It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing).”
articles.fit_reason: A named swing performance gives the subdivision question an audible setting.
articles.remaining_checks: Do not impose a fixed 2:1 ratio on the whole performance; keep the D’Angelo/J Dilla alternatives as distinct timing comparisons.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Interlock the Groove
articles.original_example_review: The eighth-note attack grid agrees with Platform Three’s D onset, A on the and of three, and explicit gaps.
articles.recommended_anchor: Fela Kuti — “Water No Get Enemy,” on _Expensive Shit_.
articles.fit_reason: Follow the division of rhythmic work among bass, percussion and higher parts.
articles.remaining_checks: Identify a short pair of interacting parts; do not imply that every attack avoids every other one.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Preserve the Distances in a Melody
articles.original_example_review: E–G–A and A–C–D preserve minor-third/major-second distances; A–B–C preserves only the broad direction.
articles.fit_reason: A familiar vocal gesture connects contour to the need for exact distances.
articles.remaining_checks: Pilot prose added. No Withers interval transcription is supplied; do not misattribute the course seed to this melody.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Establish a Tonal Home
articles.original_example_review: D Dorian and C major share a collection but organize a different center; scale color is not assigned a universal emotion.
articles.fit_reason: A clear tonal reference can be heard without assuming a conventional pop cadence.
articles.remaining_checks: Check the passage’s actual reference pitch; do not infer a key merely from a scale list.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Choose Chords by Their Notes
articles.original_example_review: The triad spellings and the C/Cm clash under an unchanged E are explicit; spacing is a separate change.
articles.recommended_anchor: Bob Marley and the Wailers — “Three Little Birds.”
articles.fit_reason: A comparatively simple song setting is a gentler entrance to triadic harmony than unexplained extended sonorities.
articles.remaining_checks: Verify the accompaniment and exact chord tones; a major triad example need not be root position in every part.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Think in Chord Numbers
articles.original_example_review: The C- and G-major family and the two-bar durations survive transposition; natural-minor notation is qualified.
articles.fit_reason: Chord numbers can describe a familiar progression independently of its absolute chord letters.
articles.remaining_checks: Check the recording’s progression and rhythm; never label it with Porch Light’s I–vi–IV–V merely because that is the course template.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Transpose the Song to Fit the Voice
articles.original_example_review: C to D moves every chord and melody pitch by two semitones; voice-range tradeoffs and neighboring key signatures are distinguished.
articles.recommended_anchor: Schubert — “An die Musik,” in high- and low-voice editions.
articles.fit_reason: Published high- and low-voice editions can demonstrate transposition more directly than two radically different arrangements.
articles.remaining_checks: Verify the chosen song in both editions and identify their actual keys; these are score editions, not a ready audio pair.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Decide Where the Harmony Arrives
articles.original_example_review: G–G, G–C and G–Am are interpreted in phrase context; a loop need not form a cadence at each turn.
articles.recommended_anchor: Mozart — Piano Sonata in C major, K 545, movement I.
articles.fit_reason: A short classical phrase ending can clarify what makes harmonic arrival contextual.
articles.remaining_checks: Select one checked cadence; do not transfer the whole classical grammar to the Bicep alternative.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Start with a Motif
articles.original_example_review: Pitch and duration jointly identify the seed; the four-bar continuation is explicitly an original sketch.
articles.fit_reason: A recognizable riff makes the small recurring unit easy to follow.
articles.remaining_checks: Keep pitch/rhythm evidence separate from guesses about the instrument producing the sound.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Give the Melody a Destination
articles.original_example_review: Shape, exact distances, register, rhythm and the intended singer’s range are distinguished.
articles.fit_reason: A melodic high point can have a structural job beyond simply being the highest note.
articles.remaining_checks: Choose a manageable phrase; do not suggest a beginner must reproduce the original singer’s register.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Support or Challenge the Melody Note
articles.original_example_review: A held A changes from an added sixth over C to a chord member over F; the comparison keeps pitch and duration fixed.
articles.recommended_anchor: Amy Winehouse — “Love Is a Losing Game.”
articles.fit_reason: One short vocal/harmony relationship can make support and tension audible.
articles.remaining_checks: Check the actual melody note and backing before supplying note labels or a harmonic reduction.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Let the Phrase Breathe
articles.original_example_review: The proposed six-beat line/two-beat gap is an alternative, not a claim about the continuous canonical verse melody.
articles.fit_reason: Vocal space can be discussed without forcing every phrase into a symmetrical two-bar model.
articles.remaining_checks: Map breaths and phrase spans in the particular performance; do not reduce ornament or delivery to a rigid template.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Write a Hook
articles.original_example_review: Instrumental seed, title phrase and bass timing are distinct possible hooks with explicit arrangement tradeoffs.
articles.recommended_anchor: Kylie Minogue — “Can't Get You Out of My Head.”
articles.fit_reason: A recurring vocal feature can hold identity while the surrounding arrangement changes.
articles.remaining_checks: Identify the focal feature and the space around it without reproducing a lyric excerpt.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Develop Without Losing the Idea
articles.original_example_review: Exact and diatonic sequencing differ; fragmentation and a held E across changing chords are separate transformations.
articles.fit_reason: A recurring musical relationship can develop inside a recognizable song.
articles.remaining_checks: Identify which figure changes and what remains; do not label every return a literal sequence.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Find the Central Idea
articles.original_example_review: The original example moves from a subject to a situation with an unresolved relationship; the chorus title has a clear job.
articles.fit_reason: A concentrated address can organize a whole lyric around one situation.
articles.remaining_checks: Discuss the relationship in original prose; do not paste lyrics or infer private biography.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Choose the Speaker
articles.original_example_review: Speaker, addressee and knowledge are separated; Porch Light retains one narrator across the canonical version.
articles.fit_reason: A clearly positioned narrator can reveal a situation through limited knowledge.
articles.remaining_checks: Treat the character as a speaker, not automatic autobiography.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Write Through Images
articles.original_example_review: Original coat/key alternatives show action and implication; the canonical note in verse two changes the story.
articles.recommended_anchor: Suzanne Vega — “Tom’s Diner,” original a cappella version on _Solitude Standing_.
articles.fit_reason: An unaccompanied observational lyric makes the contribution of concrete details easier to isolate.
articles.remaining_checks: Use the original a cappella recording, not the DNA remix; the arrangement difference matters to this teaching point.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Let Sound Support the Lyric
articles.original_example_review: Exact rhyme and vowel relationships are judged in a sung accent, not from spelling alone.
articles.fit_reason: Dense internal sound relationships can be heard alongside the pace of delivery.
articles.remaining_checks: Verify a short sound pattern without quoting extended lyrics; keep the note-count comparison in original material.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Make Speech and Melody Agree
articles.original_example_review: The title setting totals eight beats; longer content words and deliberate missetting are both allowed.
articles.fit_reason: Speech emphasis and melodic stress can be compared without prescribing one correct setting.
articles.remaining_checks: Check the actual phrase and pronunciation; apparent speech mismatch is not automatically a writing mistake.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Make the Lyric Develop
articles.original_example_review: The second-verse note and bridge admission alter the meaning of unchanged chorus words.
articles.recommended_anchor: Tracy Chapman — “Fast Car,” original album recording.
articles.fit_reason: New narrative information can change how a return is understood.
articles.remaining_checks: Map the chosen recording’s actual sections; do not assume every repeated passage has identical words.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Connect Chords with Small Moves
articles.original_example_review: C4/E4 common tones and G4 to A4 give a valid C-to-Am connection; the descending-bass variant is labeled a changed progression.
articles.fit_reason: Bass motion and upper-voice continuity deserve separate listening passes.
articles.remaining_checks: Hold detailed analysis until a short, checked voicing reduction is available; chord symbols alone do not establish voice leading.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Write a Bass Line
articles.original_example_review: Root skeleton, passing bass, inversions and a D-centered ostinato have distinct harmonic consequences.
articles.fit_reason: A low part can retain recognizable rhythm and direction rather than simply mark roots.
articles.remaining_checks: Transcribe a short bass phrase before giving note/timing labels; keep an instrumental role distinct from a chord root.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Add Color to a Working Chord
articles.original_example_review: Cmaj7/C7/Cm7, add9 versus 9, and sus versus added notes are spelled separately; melody clashes are checked.
articles.fit_reason: A short piano sonority can make added color and spacing audible.
articles.remaining_checks: Choose a bounded passage and a clearly labeled teaching reduction; do not label every non-triadic note a jazz extension.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Borrow a Chord
articles.original_example_review: Fm substitution and an expanded F–Fm–C ending have different durations; the A/A-flat conflict is named.
articles.fit_reason: A checked major/minor chord-color comparison can support the borrowing decision.
articles.remaining_checks: Hold exact Roman numerals until checked against the recording and score. Bach’s final-major-tonic alternative is a separate Picardy-third case.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Point to a Temporary Home
articles.original_example_review: E7 points to Am within the existing eight bars; D7–G and sustained G-centered context distinguish tonicization from modulation.
articles.recommended_anchor: Bach — Prelude in C major, BWV 846.
articles.fit_reason: A short applied-dominant approach can distinguish a local target from a lasting new home.
articles.remaining_checks: No candidate is ready for a precise chart yet: verify the exact chord, target, passage and recording. A generic jazz lead sheet is insufficient for the Ray Charles live take.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Change the Tonal World Deliberately
articles.original_example_review: D Dorian/natural minor, drone/pedal, transposition and modulation are not conflated.
articles.fit_reason: A relatively stable tonal reference can let texture develop without a standard functional progression.
articles.remaining_checks: Do not invent a key change to make the example fit; pitch-level modal claims need a checked passage.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Give Each Section a Purpose
articles.original_example_review: Section contributions are named before labels; refrain-based and instrumental alternatives are distinguished from the canonical chorus form.
articles.recommended_anchor: Kate Bush — “Running Up That Hill (A Deal with God).”
articles.fit_reason: Different recurring spans can carry different jobs even when material returns.
articles.remaining_checks: Prepare a version-specific section map; distinguish contribution from merely naming verse/chorus.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Make the Chorus Arrive
articles.original_example_review: The direct title request, lower syllabic pace and instrumental gap are alternatives to simply adding volume.
articles.fit_reason: A focal return can be heard through changes of emphasis and setting.
articles.remaining_checks: Use Robyn’s original recording, not the Calum Scott cover; verify the particular boundary before adding timestamps.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Make the Second Verse Count
articles.original_example_review: The second verse adds the waiting person’s note while preserving the eight-bar harmonic frame.
articles.fit_reason: New information can renew familiar musical material.
articles.remaining_checks: Confirm verse boundaries and narrative sequence; neither instrumental decoration nor new adjectives guarantees development.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Earn the Bridge
articles.original_example_review: The four-bar bridge has a specific admission, compressed syllabic pace and a tested no-bridge alternative.
articles.fit_reason: A named performance can show a contrasting passage changing the meaning of a return.
articles.remaining_checks: Hold a definitive bridge diagram until the chosen live version is mapped. A solo, breakdown or quiet passage is not automatically a bridge.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Choose a Form That Serves the Song
articles.original_example_review: The canonical form totals 52 bars; the refrain alternative and Platform Three’s arc are genuinely different whole-song choices.
articles.fit_reason: A multipart recording resists a one-size-fits-all verse/chorus/bridge template.
articles.remaining_checks: Map the whole chosen version; do not invent recurring choruses where the recording has another form.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Shape the Approach and the Ending
articles.original_example_review: The extra eight intro bars add about 23 seconds; definite ending, fade and loop behavior are different decisions.
articles.recommended_anchor: LCD Soundsystem — “Dance Yrself Clean,” full _This Is Happening_ version.
articles.fit_reason: A long approach and a later change can make pacing a whole-recording question.
articles.remaining_checks: Use the full album recording; an edited music video can remove the very lead-in being discussed.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Choose the World Around the Song
articles.original_example_review: Acoustic, electric and electronic Porch Light settings retain the phrase; Platform Three’s groove identity is protected.
articles.fit_reason: The two named Joni Mitchell recordings put sonic-setting differences in a concrete context.
articles.remaining_checks: Written comparison added with primary album links. A matched YouTube pair, passage boundaries and fuller analysis remain to be prepared; delivery and pacing also change.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Give Each Part a Job
articles.original_example_review: The role map separates attack, register, duration and focal job; deleting or delaying a part is an explicit alternative.
articles.fit_reason: A recurring sampled/arranged texture can be mapped by contributions rather than instrument names alone.
articles.remaining_checks: Distinguish audible roles from the label’s account of production history; a recording does not reveal its whole session.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Shape Energy over Time
articles.original_example_review: Density, register, pace, volume and contrast are separate energy dimensions; a reduced middle gives the return a job.
articles.fit_reason: A gradual build can make accumulation and reserved contrast audible.
articles.remaining_checks: Choose two bounded windows and name actual changed layers; do not equate energy solely with loudness.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Let the Voice Carry the Meaning
articles.original_example_review: Consonant/vowel timing, doubling and harmony are distinct; note choices remain connected to the accompaniment.
articles.fit_reason: Delivery can carry meaning beyond the written note sequence.
articles.remaining_checks: Discuss the specific performance without assigning private intention or asking the reader to imitate a difficult vocal range.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Revise the Weakest Moment
articles.original_example_review: A local arrangement edit is contrasted with simultaneous rewrites and checked in whole-song context.
articles.recommended_anchor: Radiohead — “True Love Waits,” _I Might Be Wrong_ live recording and _A Moon Shaped Pool_.
articles.fit_reason: Two realizations reveal alternatives, while Porch Light supplies the controlled one-change test.
articles.remaining_checks: Pilot prose added. Live/studio is not evidence that one isolated revision caused improvement; refine the broad windows before phrase-by-phrase analysis.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis

articles.title: Finish and Learn
articles.original_example_review: Both originals have clear minimum demo requirements; the 52-bar vocal form and 32-bar instrumental arc remain different.
articles.recommended_anchor: Billie Eilish — “everything i wanted,” with FINNEAS.

articles.fit_reason: The creators’ account directly addresses a song that nearly stayed unfinished.
articles.remaining_checks: Use the interview’s actual account of completion; the existence of a released work alone does not document why revision stopped.
articles.recommendation_status: editorial-fit-only; not a completed recording analysis
